summary: Describes extensions by which two optional fields, Key and Sequence Number, can be carried in the GRE header. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A tunnel label gets two new optional boxes. One helps identify which stream a packet belongs to, and the other keeps order.

questions: what is the gre key field
what is the gre sequence number
how does gre handle out of order packets
how to secure a gre tunnel
subtitle: Two optional GRE header fields that label traffic flows inside a tunnel and keep packets in order.

tldr.problem: The GRE header, which wraps one protocol inside another, had no way to tell separate traffic flows apart inside one tunnel or to detect lost and reordered packets.
tldr.mechanism: Two bits in the header say whether an optional 4-octet Key field and an optional 4-octet Sequence Number field follow. The Key identifies a flow, and the receiver uses the Sequence Number to discard out-of-sequence packets or to buffer briefly and restore order.
tldr.outcome: Tunnels get optional flow identification and unreliable but in-order delivery. Because injected sequence numbers enable denial of service, the RFC requires IPsec ESP or AH to protect the GRE header.

today: RFC 2890 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000. It updates RFC 2784, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, RFC 2784) wraps an arbitrary protocol inside another arbitrary network-layer protocol. This RFC describes how two fields, Key and Sequence Number, can optionally be carried in the GRE header.

The Key field is meant to identify an individual traffic flow within a tunnel. The Sequence Number field is used to maintain the order of packets within the tunnel. The RFC also defines the term silently discard: drop the datagram without further processing and without telling the sender, while SHOULD logging the error and counting the event.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel is like a pipe for packages. This adds an optional sticker to say which group a package belongs to, and a number to say its place in line.

sections.title: The Extended GRE Header
sections.content:
The extended header adds two flag bits to the first word and two optional 4-octet fields at the end. Bit 2 is Key Present: when it is 1, the Key field is in the header, otherwise it is not. Bit 3 is Sequence Number Present: when it is 1, the Sequence Number field is in the header, otherwise it is not.

These bit positions were chosen to be compatible with the older RFC 1701. Checksum and Reserved1 remain optional as before.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tick-boxes at the top of the label say whether the sticker and the number are attached. If a box is empty, that part is simply left off.

sections.title: The Key Field
sections.content:
The Key field is a four-octet number inserted by the encapsulator. How the key is obtained is beyond the scope of the document. It lets packets be handled based on context that is not in the encapsulated data, and it defines a logical traffic flow between encapsulator and decapsulator.

All packets of a flow are encapsulated with the same Key value, and the decapsulating end identifies the flow by that value.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is a colored sticker. Every parcel for the same friend gets the same color, so the receiver can sort them quickly.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Ordering
sections.content:
The Sequence Number is a four-byte field set by the encapsulator. The receiver MUST use it to establish the order in which packets were sent. The intended use is unreliable but in-order delivery. If the Key bit is set, the sequence number belongs to the flow named by the Key. Packets without the sequence bit can be interleaved with packets that have it.

The value runs from 0 to (232)-1, the first datagram is sent with 0, and the counter is free running modulo 232. The receiver remembers the last successfully decapsulated number and, when the tunnel is established, sets it to (232)-1.

  • Out of sequence: a number less than or equal to the last one, meaning it lies in the last number and the preceding 231-1 values. The decapsulator SHOULD silently discard it.
  • In sequence: exactly 1 greater (modulo 232), or a packet with no sequence number. It is decapsulated.
  • Gap: anything else. The receiver may buffer packets sorted by sequence number and release them when the missing one arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets a number in line. If a parcel with an old number shows up late, it is thrown away. If one is skipped, the receiver may wait a moment for it.

sections.title: Buffering Limits and When to Use It
sections.content:
No packet may wait in the reordering buffer longer than OUTOFORDER_TIMER milliseconds. After that, the receiver MUST walk the buffer in sorted order and decapsulate packets, ignoring gaps, until none have waited that long. The receiver may also cap each per-flow buffer at MAX_PERFLOW_BUFFER packets; when a new packet would exceed it, the packet at the head of the buffer is decapsulated right away. The RFC does not give values for these two constants.

Sequencing should be used with care. It is a good idea to avoid it when the tunneled protocol already has in-order delivery or tolerates reordering. If only some traffic needs order, only those packets need the sequence bit set. A small reordering buffer can help when a higher layer uses stateful compression or encryption, since packet loss resets that state.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver only waits so long for a missing parcel, and only keeps so many waiting. After that it moves on so the line never gets stuck.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With the Sequence Number field, an attacker can inject packets with arbitrary sequence numbers and launch a denial of service attack. To protect against this, IP security protocols MUST be used to protect the GRE header and the tunneled payload. Either ESP or AH MUST be used. ESP protects the IP payload, which includes the GRE header. AH authenticates the entire packet other than mutable fields.

Despite its name, the Key field is not involved in any sort of security.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could slip in fake numbered parcels to jam the line. So the whole tunnel must be locked with proper security. The sticker called key is just a label, not a lock.

viz.caption: HOW THE RECEIVER CLASSIFIES A SEQUENCE NUMBER

items.title: Out of sequence
items.text: Less than or equal to the last decapsulated number. Silently discarded.

items.title: In sequence
items.text: Exactly 1 greater, modulo 2**32, or no sequence number. Decapsulated.

items.title: Gap
items.text: Neither of the above. May be buffered until the missing packet arrives or the timer expires.
